stops.name: Bradbury Building
stops.teaser: A plain brick box hiding a five-story glass court and open-cage elevators.
stops.map: Bradbury Building, 304 S Broadway, Los Angeles, CA
stops.clue: Go downtown to Broadway and 3rd Street and find the plain-looking brick building with an arched entrance. Step inside the lobby court if it is open.
stops.safety: Downtown is busy. Use crosswalks. The building has offices, so be quiet and follow posted visiting rules.

then.line: The Bradbury Building in 1894, the year it was finished.

now.label: The court today

story: The Bradbury Building was built in 1893 and finished in 1894 at a cost of $500,000, about three times its original $175,000 budget. Lewis L. Bradbury, a mining and real estate millionaire, began planning it in 1892 and died that year, some months before it opened.

Bradbury first hired Sumner Hunt, then dismissed his design and hired George Wyman, a draftsman who earned $5 a week and had no formal architecture training. Wikipedia says there is no concrete evidence that Wyman changed Hunt's design, which is why some people dispute who the true architect was.

The five-story central court has a skylight, open bird-cage elevators, wrought-iron grillwork made in France and shown at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, and yellow and pink brick. It was a National Historic Landmark in 1977 and appears in Blade Runner (1982).
stops.disputed: Who is the true architect is a long argument. Hunt drew the plans, but Wyman built it and Wikipedia says it is unclear what he changed.

claims.t: The Bradbury Building was completed in the 1890s.
George Wyman was a famous architect when he got the job.
claims.why: He was a draftsman earning $5 a week with no formal training.

spot.q: The 1894 photo shows the Bradbury Building when it opened. It was budgeted at $175,000. About how much did it cost to build?
spot.why: It cost $500,000, about three times its original $175,000 budget.

stops.name: Hollywood Sign
stops.teaser: A giant real estate ad that became a symbol.
stops.map: Lake Hollywood Park, Los Angeles, CA
stops.clue: Find a public viewing spot, such as Lake Hollywood Park or an overlook in Griffith Park, where you can see the white letters on the hillside. Do not try to climb to the sign.
stops.safety: The sign is on a protected hillside and hiking up to it is not allowed. View it from a distance. Park legally, stay quiet near homes and do not block narrow residential streets.

story: The sign was built in 1923. It originally read "Hollywoodland." Los Angeles Times publisher Harry Chandler built it as a billboard advertising his upscale Hollywoodland real estate development.
Each letter was about 43 feet tall and 30 feet wide. The original sign was lit by 4,000 20-watt light bulbs spaced 8 inches apart.
It was never meant to last. It became a symbol of the film industry that grew up around it.
stops.fact: The original sign had 4,000 light bulbs.
stops.disputed: Nothing big is disputed here. The popular guess is that it was built for the movie business, but it was built to sell houses.

claims.t: The Hollywood Sign was first built as an advertisement for a housing development.
claims.why: The Hollywood Sign Trust: Harry Chandler built it in 1923 to advertise Hollywoodland.

claims.t: The Hollywood Sign was built to honor the film industry.
claims.why: It was a real estate billboard. Its meaning came later.

sources.t: Hollywood Sign Trust: A sign is born

spot.q: The 1920s photo shows the sign when it read 'Hollywoodland'. In what year was it built?
spot.why: Harry Chandler built the sign in 1923 as a billboard for his Hollywoodland development.

stops.name: Angels Flight
stops.teaser: The world's shortest railway, with two cars named Olivet and Sinai.
stops.map: Angels Flight Railway, 351 S Hill St, Los Angeles, CA
stops.clue: Go downtown to Hill Street near Grand Central Market and find the tiny orange-and-black funicular with two cars.
stops.safety: Hill Street is busy. Use crosswalks. Check the funicular's status first, because it has closed many times.
stops.field: Field notes pending: nobody has walked this stop for the app yet.

q.prompt: What are the two cars named?
q.verify: Wikipedia says the cars are named Olivet and Sinai. Read the cars on site. Written from sources, not yet checked on site.

then.label: The funicular then
then.line: The funicular on October 2, 1960, nine years before it closed.

link.t: Look for historic photos at the Library of Congress

now.head: Today
now.label: The funicular today
now.line: The two cars run on a short track on Hill Street.

story: Angels Flight opened in 1901 as the Los Angeles Incline Railway, financed by Colonel J. W. Eddy. It has about 298 feet of track with a 96-foot rise, a grade of about 33 percent. The two cars, Olivet and Sinai, run in opposite directions on a shared cable.
The railway closed in May 1969 for Bunker Hill redevelopment, and the cars sat in storage for 27 years. It reopened on February 24, 1996 at a new site half a block south.

On February 1, 2001, the car Sinai rolled downhill uncontrolled and hit Olivet. One 83-year-old man died and eight others were hurt. The NTSB blamed improper design and construction of the drive system. It reopened in 2010, closed again, and reopened in 2017.
stops.fact: It is Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument No. 4.
stops.disputed: "World's shortest railway" is a plaque's wording: "said to be the world's shortest incorporated railway." Treat it as a claim.

claims.t: Angels Flight has always stayed at its original site.
claims.why: It closed in 1969 and reopened in 1996 half a block south.

sources.t: Los Angeles Public Library: Angels Flight

spot.q: Angels Flight closed in May 1969 and reopened on February 24, 1996. For about how many years did the cars sit in storage?
spot.why: The cars sat in storage for 27 years, from 1969 to 1996.

stops.teaser: The oldest part of Los Angeles, with the oldest house still standing.
stops.clue: Walk across from Union Station to the brick-paved marketplace street beside the old Plaza.
stops.safety: The street is crowded and has uneven bricks. Use crosswalks to cross Main and Alameda, and watch for kids and carts.

story: Spanish settlers founded Los Angeles in 1781: 11 families, 44 people, plus a few soldiers, on a site southeast of today's Olvera Street. The street's early names included Placita Olvera and Wine Street. In 1877 a City Council ordinance renamed Wine Street for Agustín Olvera, the first Superior Court judge of Los Angeles County.

The Avila Adobe was built in 1818 by Francisco Ávila at 10 Olvera Street. It is described as the oldest surviving residence in Los Angeles. Christine Sterling began her campaign to save the area in 1926, and the street opened on Easter Sunday 1930 as Paseo de Los Angeles.

David Siqueiros's mural América Tropical was unveiled above the street in 1932 and soon covered up because of its politics. The Getty Conservation Institute began conservation work in 2010, and an interpretive center opened in 2012. The area is El Pueblo de Los Ángeles Historical Monument.
stops.fact: The Avila Adobe was built in 1818.
stops.disputed: Some critics call the street a sanitized tourist version of Mexican culture, and Wikipedia says so. The oldest brick house claim for the Pelanconi House also lists two different dates.

claims.t: The Avila Adobe is the oldest surviving residence in Los Angeles.
Olvera Street was built by the original 1781 settlers as a market.
claims.why: It opened as a marketplace on Easter Sunday 1930.

spot.q: Christine Sterling began her campaign to save the area in 1926, and the street opened on Easter Sunday 1930. About how many years did that take?
